entries.answer: Deepfake fraud is now routine: identity-verification firm Entrust detected a deepfake attempt every five minutes in 2024. Scammers use AI-generated faces and video in romance and investment scams as well as attacks on businesses. Because people can't reliably spot deepfakes by eye, check suspicious images with a detector and verify identities on a live video call.

Sextortion is rising fast and mostly targets teenage boys. Thorn's analysis of NCMEC CyberTipline data found an average of 812 sextortion reports per week, and 90% of victims in those reports were male, aged 14 to 17. AI-generated fake nudes mean scammers no longer need a real image to threaten someone.

Faux Spy adds one to your browser's right-click menu: check any photo on any site without uploading it, and get a verdict with a confidence score in about two seconds. entries.answer: An AI video detector checks whether a video was generated by AI tools such as Sora, Runway, Pika, Veo or Kling. With Faux Spy Pro + Video, right-click a video in your browser to get a frame-by-frame verdict and the likely generator, without uploading anything. AI video is harder to judge by eye than a still image, so a detector plus a check of the source is the safest approach.

entries.answer: To stay safe on dating apps, confirm a match is real before you invest time or money: check their photos, insist on a video call, and never send money to someone you haven't met. AI-generated profiles and pig-butchering investment scams are the biggest newer risks. Meet in public, tell a friend your plans, and report any profile that asks for money or crypto.

entries.answer: The biggest romance-scam warning signs are a match who moves fast emotionally, avoids video calls or meeting, and eventually asks for money, gift cards or crypto. Other early signs include photos that look too polished, pressure to leave the dating app, and stories about emergencies abroad. Treat anyone you've never met in person who asks for money as a likely scammer.

entries.answer: Catfishing is creating a fake online identity to deceive someone, usually into a romantic relationship, for money, attention or exploitation. Catfish use stolen photos or, increasingly, AI-generated faces that don't belong to any real person. Warning signs include refusing video calls, inconsistent stories and requests for money.

entries.answer: A deepfake is an image, video or audio clip generated or altered by AI to look real. Deepfakes are used in romance scams, impersonation fraud and disinformation, and modern ones are hard to spot by eye. Detection tools analyze the media itself for signs of AI generation.

entries.answer: Social Catfish and Faux Spy solve different problems: Social Catfish searches for where a photo has appeared before, while Faux Spy checks whether a photo was generated by AI. Reverse image search catches stolen real photos, but an AI-generated face has no earlier copies to find. For a suspicious dating profile, using both covers both kinds of fake.

entries.answer: If you need to catch AI-generated profile photos, a reverse image search service like Social Catfish isn't enough, because AI faces have no earlier copies online. An AI image detector such as Faux Spy (free for 3 scans a day) checks the photo itself. For stolen real photos, reverse image search is still the right tool, so the two work best together.

entries.answer: The clearest signs someone is catfishing you are that they won't video chat, their story has gaps, and they eventually ask for money. Early on, look for a thin profile with polished photos and a push to move off the app; later come excuses for not meeting and sudden emergencies. Checking their photos for AI generation or theft is the fastest way to confirm.

entries.answer: Catfish scams follow a script: build a fake profile, move the conversation off the dating app, build an emotional bond over weeks, then ask for money. Many end in a fake investment pitch, known as pig butchering, or a "recovery" scam aimed at people who were already defrauded. The best time to interrupt the script is before the conversation leaves the app.

entries.answer: Deepfake scams use AI-generated photos, video or voice to impersonate someone you trust or to invent a person who doesn't exist. In romance scams, a fake identity built from AI images is used to win trust before asking for money; Americans reported $672 million in romance and confidence-scam losses to the FBI in 2024. Verify on a live video call and check suspicious images with a detector.

entries.answer: To tell if a photo is AI-generated, look closely at hands, lighting, backgrounds and edges, then run it through an AI image detector. Older generators leave obvious mistakes, but newer ones often don't, so a visual check alone isn't reliable. A detector analyzes pixel-level patterns your eye can't see.

entries.answer: Romance scammers use stolen photos of real people or, increasingly, AI-generated faces of people who don't exist. Americans reported $672 million in romance and confidence-scam losses to the FBI in 2024. Check suspicious photos with a reverse image search for stolen images and an AI detector for generated ones.

entries.answer: Reverse image search finds stolen real photos; an AI detector catches faces that were generated by AI. You need both. An AI-generated face has no earlier copies online, so reverse search comes up empty, while a stolen real photo won't look AI-generated to a detector. Run both checks on any suspicious profile.

entries.answer: AI-generated profile pictures are faces created by image generators, not photos of real people, and they're now common on dating apps and social media. Scammers and fake accounts use them because they're free, unique and can't be traced with reverse image search. A detector that analyzes the image itself is the most reliable way to spot one.

entries.answer: To tell if a video is AI-generated, watch the motion rather than single frames: look for objects that morph, hands and text that change between frames, and physics that doesn't add up. Modern generators like Sora and Runway can produce frames that look real on their own, so a dedicated video detector is more reliable than metadata or a visual check.
